narr: Welcome to Week 5 of our Computer Science course in C. This week, we'll learn how to make our programs make decisions and repeat tasks using control structures.
We'll cover blocks and compound statements, conditional statements like if/else if/else and switch, and various types of loops like while, for, and do-while.
We'll also explore break and continue statements, and touch on functions, modular programming, and variable scope.

data.heading: Blocks and Compound Statements
bullets: A simple statement ends with a semicolon
Multiple statements combined into a compound statement (block) with curly braces
A block can stand where a simple statement is expected
Blocks are compiled as a single unit
Variables can be declared inside blocks
Blocks can be nested inside each other

narr: Let's start with blocks and compound statements. In C, a simple statement ends with a semicolon, like z equals foo of x plus y.
When you need to combine multiple statements, you use a compound statement, also called a block, which is enclosed in curly braces.
A block can be used anywhere a simple statement is expected, and the compiler treats it as a single unit.
You can declare variables inside blocks, which limits their scope to that block.
Blocks can be nested inside each other, allowing for structured and organized code.

data.heading: Nested Blocks Example

narr: Here's an example of nested blocks. We first declare an integer variable temp and initialize it with x plus y.
Then we assign the result of foo(temp) to z.
Inside this block, we have another nested block where we declare a float variable temp2 and initialize it with x times y.
Finally, we add the result of bar(temp2) to z.

data.heading: Conditionals in C: if/else if/else
bullets: C89/C90 has no boolean type; C99 has bool via <stdbool.h>
Conditions are expressions that evaluate to non-zero (true) or zero (false)
if: execute statement if condition is true
else: execute statement if condition is false
else if: provides additional alternative paths

narr: Now let's explore conditional statements in C. Unlike C++ or Java, C89/C90 doesn't have a built-in boolean type.
In C99, you can use bool by including the stdbool.h header.
Conditions are expressions that evaluate to non-zero for true or zero for false.
The if statement executes its inner statement if the condition is true.
The else statement executes its inner statement if the condition is false.
The else if statement provides additional alternative paths, checking conditions in order until the first true one is found.
Let's look at some examples of conditional statements. First, we have a simple if statement that checks if x is odd.
Next, we have an if-else structure that handles both even and odd cases of x.
Finally, we have a more complex example with else if that handles multiple conditions based on the remainder when x is divided by 4.

data.heading: Nested if Pitfall
bullets: Without braces, else associates with the nearest inner if
Use curly braces to control which if an else belongs to

narr: A common pitfall with nested if statements is the association of else with the wrong if.
Without braces, else automatically associates with the nearest inner if statement.
To attach else to an outer if, you need to use curly braces to create a block.

data.heading: Nested if Example

narr: In this first example, the else belongs to the inner if, which might not be the intended logic.
In the second example, by adding curly braces, we've made the else associate with the outer if statement.
This subtle difference can significantly change the behavior of your program, so be careful with nested ifs.

data.heading: Switch Statement
bullets: Alternative to if/else if ladders for equality checks
Takes an integer or character variable
Cases are different entry points into the block

narr: The switch statement provides an alternative to if/else if ladders, especially useful for equality checks.
It takes an integer or character variable as input and considers cases for its value.
Each case label acts as a different entry point into the block.
When a case matches, the code executes until the nearest break statement.
Without break, execution falls through to the next case.
The default case acts as the 'otherwise' branch when no other cases match.

data.heading: Switch Example: Grade Evaluation

narr: Here's a comparison between an if/else if ladder and a switch statement for evaluating grades.
The if/else if version checks each condition sequentially, which can be less efficient and more verbose.
The switch version is more concise and efficient for this type of equality checking.
Each equality check becomes a case label, and the else becomes the default case.
Remember to include break statements to prevent fall-through to the next case.

data.heading: Multiple Case Labels

narr: Switch statements can handle multiple case labels for the same code block.
In the first example, we have separate cases for 'Y' and 'N'.
In the second example, we've combined 'Y' and 'y' into a single case, allowing the same code to execute for both uppercase and lowercase 'Y'.

data.heading: Example 6.1: Melody from a Name
data.problem: Create a program that reads a character at a time, calculates the ASCII code modulo 7, and prints the corresponding note name.
steps: Check for successful input and sentinel character #
Select and print the corresponding note
Repeat until EOF or # is encountered

narr: Let's look at a practical example from the lab: creating a melody from a name.
The program reads one character at a time, calculates the ASCII code modulo 7, and prints the corresponding note name.
For example, the character 'A' has an ASCII code of 65.
65 modulo 7 equals 2, which corresponds to the note C.
In the lab version, there's an intentional bug: the break statement is missing after case 2.
This causes fall-through, so input A# would print C, then D.
To fix this, we need to add a break statement after the printf in case 2.
The program continues reading characters until it encounters EOF or the sentinel character #.

The ASCII code for 'A' is 65.
